title: Two regimes? Compare the relationship before and after a known date
concepts: economic reading of a regime change

explain.prompt: In 5–7 sentences: how did the Brent–WTI relationship change on 1 January 2016 (spread level, spread volatility, short-run pass-through)? Each sub-period is strongly cointegrated, yet the full 2012–2019 sample is not (Engle-Granger p ≈ 0.28). Explain why, and what you would have concluded if you had only run the test on the full sample. Why must the break date come from outside the data?
rubric: Before 2016 the WTI discount averaged ≈ 0.17 log points (≈ 16 %), after ≈ 0.06 (≈ 6 %); the spread is less volatile after; the daily pass-through (return β) rises from ≈ 0.59 to ≈ 0.89 and the return correlation from ≈ 0.79 to ≈ 0.88.

Economic reading: with the export ban, WTI was landlocked and partly priced off local US balances; once exports were allowed, arbitrage tied it more tightly to Brent — a smaller discount and a closer daily link.

Each regime is cointegrated (EG p ≈ 0 in both), but one regression over 2012–2019 forces a single equilibrium; the residual inherits the shift in the equilibrium level and looks non-stationary, so EG fails to reject (p ≈ 0.28).

A full-sample test alone would wrongly conclude 'no long-run relationship' (or, with another sample, a relationship with a wrong β): a structural break distorts cointegration tests just as it distorts ADF.
The date must be chosen a priori from an identifiable event (the end of the export ban); choosing it by scanning the data for the largest change would invalidate the usual test statistics.
Consequence: estimate and use the relationship within the current regime, and re-test it regularly on recent data.
